utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Good morning to counsel. We can resume for this final day of the week. Is this a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I have no request for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is Mr. Miroslav Pejcinovic? You don't have to give us a summary, because we have one, I even have it in French. Have Mr. Miroslav Pejcinovic brought in, please. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, while remaining standing, please tell us your name, your given name, your age, your profession, your residence, and then you will read the solemn declaration which all witnesses testifying before this Tribunal read. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Pejcinovic. I am 36 years old, I was born in 1962 in Vares. I am a graduated engineer of mining. I lived in Vares up until the war and was then a refugee in Seljanko (phoen), and in 1997 I returned to Vares. I am married, I am the father of two children, and at present I work as the deputy of the police administration for Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please remain standing for a few more moments, as long as it takes to read your solemn declaration that the usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You have agreed to testify at the request of the Defence as part of the trial initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY against General Blaskic, who at that time was a Colonel and who is in the courtroom now. You're going first to answer the questions that Defence counsel asks you, and then the questions asked by the Office of the Prosecutors, and finally by the Judges. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please. Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, you have already introduced yourself, but would you please add something by telling us what you did before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war I worked in the steel mine of Vares, and I was the head engineer for pit exploitation. And at the elections in 1990 I was elected as deputy to the assembly of the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court, and it would be a good idea if you could take the pointer and show us what I'm going to ask you on the map, tell us where the municipality of Vares is located, what the neighbouring municipalities are, how far, for example, the town of Vares is from Sarajevo and Kiseljak, some towns that we're already well acquainted with, and after that we're going to go over to discuss the population according to the latest population census. So while you're sitting in front of the microphone, please tell, describe this to us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Vares is a municipality which is located in Central Bosnia, geographically viewed it is located 50 kilometres northeast of Sarajevo, and the road to the town of Vares separates Tortu (phoen), the junction is on the main road to Sarajevo, it is some 60 kilometres away from -- and the neighbouring municipalities to the south are the municipality of Breza, to the west or the southwest we have the municipality of Visoko, west is Kakanj, and northwest is Zavidovici, to the north and northeast the municipality of Olovo and to the southeast and east the Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point the town of Vares out to us on the map? I hope we can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find Vares, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, please resume your seat. So we don't have Vares on this particular map, but we're going to bring maps which will show Vares in the course of our examination-in-chief. Tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Pejcinovic, the number of inhabitants of the municipality of Vares, and you can use your notes, the number according to the latest population census from 1991 and the relationship between the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the population census of 1991 in the municipality of Vares there were 22.203 inhabitants. Of that number 9.014 were Croats, or percentage wise, 40.6 per cent. There were 6.714 Bosniaks or 13.2 per cent. There were 3.644 Serbs or 16.42 per cent. And those who belonged to the miscellaneous group, 2.892, or 12.74 per cent, and they were, for the most part, those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask to you speak a little more slowly, please. Would you explain to the Court, the first democratic elections were held in 1994. How did they evolve?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you sure about those percentages? 6.700 are 13.2 per cent, I'm not very good at arithmetic, but I think there must be a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: 30.32 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a mistake in the translation, 30.2 per cent. Or in the transcript, I beg your pardon, probably not in the translation, in the transcript. So as you say, the elections were held in 1990, what were the results of the first democratic elections?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: After the first democratic elections the municipal assembly of Vares numbered 50 deputies. Of that number the most seats were won by the SDP 19, the Social Democratic Party; 13 went to the Croatian Democratic Community, the HDZ; nine seats went to the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action; eight seats went to the former Reformist Alliance, the alliance of reformist forces of Mr. Ante Markovic; and one seat went to the DSS, Rasim Kadic, that is a youth organisation, a youth party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did Vares differ from practically all the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, in Vares the social democratic parties won the elections and not the nationalist parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In all 190 communes before the war in Bosnia Herzegovina, of that number in Vares the Social Democratic Party won, which is the only one; whereas, in the other municipalities the nationalist parties came to head them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the results of these elections, how was the authority set up in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The executive power and legal authorities were formed in conformity with the results of the election results and the population census dating back from 1981. And so the first position, that is to say, the president of the municipal assembly of Vares, went to the SDP, and this post was performed by Mr. Dario Andrijevic from the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Social Democratic Party, that is what you mean, the SDP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second post of executive pound authority, the president of the executive board, or the municipal government, went to the Croatian democratic community, and that post was performed by Mr. Zvonimir Dugonjic, and a candidate from the Croat ethnic group. The third post of vice-president of the municipal assembly of Vares, which was an amateur voluntary post, not a professional post, went to the party of democratic action, the SDA party, and this function was performed by Ms. Mervana Hadjimurtezic, she was a member of the Bosniak ethnic group. And the fourth post, vice-president of the municipal government went to the SDP, the Social Democratic Party, and that post was filled by Mr. Radko Gajic, and he was a member of the Serb ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, once again we have been cautioned to slow down. Would you try to speak a little more slowly, please. Mr. Pejcinovic, explain to the Trial Chamber now which functions you held beginning with 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections in November, 1992, I was elected deputy to the municipal assembly of Vares, and I was also elected president of the club of the deputies of the HDZ in the municipality of Vares. When the first signs of war came in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decision of the municipal assembly of Vares, in April 1992, appointed me deputy commander of the municipal staff for the Defence of Vares for informatics and information. And I performed this function in the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipal staff for defence of Vares, this was a joint organ of the Muslims, Croats, that is to say, all the inhabitants of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but it was appointed by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So carry on. You were saying on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of July, 1992, when the Croat defence council, as an executive organ of power and authority was set up, I performed the function of a member of the executive council of the HVO in the municipality with regard to housing matters, and in the operative part of the HVO, in the presidency of the HVO, I was one of the five members of the presidency of the HVO in Vares. I performed this duty until the 18th of October, 1993 when, with a convoy of refugees, I left Vares and went in the direction of Herzegovina. When I returned to Kiseljak, because Vares, in the meantime, was under the control of the BH army, on the 26th of November, 1993, I took over the duty of the deputy of the Croatian assembly of Vares for Vares with its headquarters in Kiseljak. I performed this function up to the 1st of April, 1994, whereby, by a decision of the president of the assembly of Herceg-Bosna, I was appointed the president of the municipal assembly of Vares, and I performed this function right up until the establishment of the joint pound authority on the 3rd of February, 1998. And from the 10th of February, 1998 I am the deputy of the chief of police in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a federal police force and it is combined for the Bosnian Croat police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a Bosnian Croat police force, and in that joint police force every six months I rotate with my colleague, a Bosniak, as chief of the police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, briefly, and tell the Trial Chamber briefly, something about the development of political relations in Vares, because the situation was rather specific there compared to the other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and actually even before that, in 1991, due to the circumstances involved, we had a lot of heavy industry there, and in 1991 they ceased to operate. The situation in Vares was very difficult. Basic food supplies were scarce, so it was difficult for the population to survive. Then the Croatian democratic community took action to bring in considerable humanitarian aid from Croatia and to distribute it equitably among the entire population of Vares. This situation prevailed at the beginning of 1992 also because the SDP, as a Social Democratic Party, did have power, was in government in Vares, but they could not establish contact at all with the higher authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina because nationalist forces were in power there. So they didn't have the right kind of links. And they couldn't even provide the basic supplies for the population, and also medical supplies, so that the health centre could function properly. And also for public utilities, public transportation, et cetera. Then the president of the municipal assembly, Mr. Dario Janjovic asked through the municipal prime minister, he asked the HDZ to try to do something about this, to bring in certain quantities of the resources needed for the normal functioning of Vares. And then, in 1992, already the first convoy started going towards Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation like with the army? What about the military component within the municipality, how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, after the well-known events in Sarajevo, an extraordinary session of the municipal assembly of Vares was convened, and a decision was reached to establish a joint staff for the defence of the municipality of Vares. At that assembly, Mr. Borivoje Malbasic, a Croat, was appointed president of this staff. It was a mixed staff consisting of Muslims and Croats. The units that were under the command of this staff were units of the HVO and of the Territorial Defence, and they primarily functioned according to territorial principle in the villages. And one can say that 90 per cent of the members of these units belonged to a single national group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please tell the Court now what happened afterwards, and how did this split occur between the Bosniaks and the Croats in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned that in May there were intensive negotiations between the HDZ and the SDP that had held most of the power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at the level of Vares, they gave up their power. A joint authority was set up with the participation of both Bosniaks and Muslims because the representatives of the Serb people had already withdrawn. And then in April 1992, a part of the Serbian villages reached a decision that they would secede from Vares and they would become part of the municipality of Ilijas. So those who remained wanted to have a joint authority, and a meeting was held with the representatives of the SDA so that we could agree on this joint authority. At this meeting, an executive branch of the government was supposed to be established. The Croatian Democratic Immunity wanted this to be called the Croatian Defence Council, and the Bosniak side proposed that this should be the War Presidency of the Municipality of Vares. The negotiations were painstaking and difficult because it was difficult to reconcile such different views. Ultimately, the president of the SDA for Vares, Mr. Avdija Kovacevic, said that they realised that the Croats could do a lot more in this kind of situation and that they could accept this kind of executive government but that they could not allow it to be called the Croatian Defence Council. Let it be called the Defence Council of the Municipality of Vares, so that was about it. After these unsuccessful negotiations, at the end of June 1992, the crisis staff of the Croatian Defence Community that was functioning in Vares reached a decision to establish the independent authority of the Croatian Defence Council, which was established in Vares as at the 1st of July, 1992 as the executive government of the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this mean, in fact, for the municipality, for the enterprises, the companies there? Were there any pledges of allegiance? Did people have to sign such papers? Were people laid off?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was laid off from the municipal authorities or anywhere. No one was left jobless, except that certain directors of enterprises expressed their support in writing to this government because, during the first days of this government, they felt that there was a drastic change, and that is as compared to the government of the SDP because the routes towards Herzegovina and Croatia were opened, and all the necessary supplies were obtained, as well as humanitarian aid in the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the political leaders of the Bosniak people react to this or, rather, the representatives of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as this government was established, that is to say, on the 6th of July, 1992, a meeting was convened of the representatives of the then established government of the Croatian Defence Council with the representatives of political parties that participate in the assembly of the municipality of Vares. At this meeting, from the Bosniak side, Mr. Avdija Kovacevic was present, that is, the president of the SDA, and Ms. Mervana Hadjimurtezic, the vice-president of the assembly of the municipality of Vares. An attempt was made to work out a compromise, that the HVO would keep the executive branch and that all parties should set up a presidency of the municipality of Vares and that an assembly should be convened of the municipality of Vares and that these decisions should be verified. However, the Bosniak side did not agree to this, and on the next day, the 7th of July, 1992, they established the War Presidency of the Municipality of Vares in the village of Strijezevo within the municipality of Vares. That's where their seat was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, there was a division of political power. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: There was a division of political power and, as a result of that, on the 9th of July, 1992, there was a division in the joint staff of the municipality of Vares, which was a joint staff until then. Afterwards, the Croats established their Municipal Staff of the HVO of Vares, and the Bosniaks established their staff in the village of Dabravine towards Breza, all within the municipality of Vares too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the police, what about the police, was it a joint force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The police still functioned as a joined force, except that the commander was replaced, the commander of the police station in Vares. But the police continued to function because Bosniak policemen continued to work with their Croat colleagues, and this situation went on until October 1992 when, in the village of Dabravine, a police patrol of the police station of Vares was attacked and disarmed. The Croats were sent to Vares, and then the Bosniaks set up their own public security station with their seat in Dabravine for the municipality of Vares. And now the civilian authority, that is, the War Presidency, also moved to the village of Dobravina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a complete division in terms of all forms of power. What about the citizens, what about companies, what about people who were employed there, did this division of power have any effect on the life of the ordinary citizens of the municipality of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: One can say that this did not affect their lives at all. All of those who lived in the town of Vares until then, regardless of whether they were Bosniaks or Croats, continued to live in their apartments, in their houses. There were no incidents whatsoever. All of those people who were directors of various companies continued to be directors, and those who were employees continued to be employees, and those who were in the units of the HVO and the Territorial Defence were still registered in their companies but as if they were on a waiting list, that is to say, they were registered in these units, but this did not mean that they lost their jobs. In 1992, we also took Bosniak refugees from Sokolac and Han-Pijesak, Bosnian municipalities. We put them up in the collection centre. And even after this division of government, they stayed on, and the Croat Defence Council took care of them and supplied humanitarian aid to them. And this was the situation until the first conflicts broke out in 1993 in the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, were there any conflicts between Bosniaks and Croats in your area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No. In January 1993, I said, and you also mentioned, that there were two governments, the Croat and the Bosniak, but there were no conflicts. And in August and September, there were problems with the passage of convoys taking humanitarian aid that were going to Vares. As they passed through the village of Dabravine, they were stopped there and they were not given safe passage through the part that was under HVO control. And as a result of these problems, the Croats built a road in the direction of Kraljeva Sutjeska in the municipality of Kakanj, and then they brought these two roads together, and everything went through this way, through the municipality of Kakanj. But the situation was peaceful, although there were Bosniaks in these villages too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in April 1993 when the Bosniak Croat conflict occurred in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in April in 1993 when, in Central Bosnia, conflicts start, Vares was completely surrounded. There were no roads that were open for receiving humanitarian aid in Vares. However, as opposed to all other areas in the municipality of Vares, there were no conflicts and there were no incidents. The situation was quite peaceful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were frontlines established between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The only decision that was reached by the HVO of Vares was that, as the conflict broke out, because our police kept sending reports from Pajto Han, that checkpoint, that Bosniaks from the village of Bugozevo (phoen) were going to the frontline towards Kiseljak to prohibit the passage of uniformed persons belonging to the Territorial Defence, and also they were not allowed to walk around the town of Vares, but frontlines were not established yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the first incident break out between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The first incident between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in Vares occurred on the 1st of June, 1993 when a sniper in the Lijesnica valley killed Mario Miocevic, an HVO soldier. However, one must say that this was an incident that did not cause any reactions on the Croatian side. The situation remained to be peaceful, and there was no revenge. There was no reaction of this sort. Everything remained as it was beforehand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court what happened on the 13th of June, 1993 on the day of St. Ante in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, 1993, it was a Sunday, it was a holiday of the St. Ante, and many Croat refugees came from the Kakanj municipality and from the parish of Kraljeva Sutjeska. In one day, between 13.000 and 14.000 Croats arrived in Vares. Everything collapsed. There was a total blockade. People came in different ways. As I said, through the village of Kopjari, which was the only way they could come, that is the way they came, and also they walked over the hill of Perun, and these were streams of refugees that were coming in. And the municipal HVO immediately established special duty service, and we put up these refugees in sports centres, in gyms, specifically, in the elementary school and high school, and in the reserve parts factory and the ready-make clothing factory, in the village of Borovici, in different factories. This is simply to say that the entire town collapsed and nothing could function normally any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the 13.000 to 14.000 Croats who came as refugees from Kakanj and Kraljeva Sutjeska, did the people of Travnik come as well? If so, how many and via which territory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day in the evening of the 13th of June, 700 to 800 people from Travnik, recruits which the Serbs from the camp of Manjaca transferred to Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the refugees tell you? Why did they start moving? Why did so many columns of people start moving from the municipality of Kakanj, Kraljeva Sutjeska, and Travnik? What had happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The people coming from Kakanj carrying bundles said they were attacked by MOS, the BH army, and that their villages were being attacked and shelled and that they were frightened, that there were a lot of them, and that they were crying "Allah-u-ekber" and cries of that kind. In Kraljeva Sutjeska grenades were falling. It was being shelled. Some of them took refuge in the Franciscan monastery there, but the majority of people fled towards Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us whether the authorities succeeded in securing the Muslim property and emptying Muslim flats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Although there was a whole river flow of 13.000 to 14.000 refugees from Krajleva Sukica and Kakanj, and although there were many flats which were empty and closed and held by the members of the BH army, the military and civilian police of the HVO in Vares, led by Mr. Zvonko Duznovic did not allow anybody to take up residence in these flats. There were several attempts to break into the flats, but as soon as reports of this kind reached the police station, people were thrown out and the flats were maintained as they had been before this influx of refugees, and these were mostly empty flats; whereas none of the Bosniaks in the town were maltreated or thrown out of their flats. The refugees were sent to collective centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vares at that time, the police and military forces of the HVO were not able to offer protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the municipality of Vares, the war had not started yet. The situation was tense, but the HVO in Vares did not allow people from Kakanj to undertake any actions of retaliation, but they tried to negotiate with the municipality of Visoko because people had come from Sasnivuci (phoen), these villages from around Visoko, to have part of the refugees go back to where they had come from, but this was aborted. This attempt did not succeed. This relationship towards the Bosniak property, the HVO in Vares was to enter a conflict situation with the people of Kakanj, and this was reflected later on when the Croats from Vares went to Kiseljak as refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Vares had been completely surrounded but that there was no war, that is to say, there was no shooting. In a situation of this kind, when it found itself totally encircled by the Muslims and Serbs, how did Vares solve its supply problems?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: At first, the situation was extremely difficult. We lacked basic food stuffs. The refugees were handed out a daily one-quarter of a loaf of bread and some food. Very small quantities of food were given for the children and the elderly because there were no stocks. In a situation of this kind, there was general dissatisfaction amongst the refugees, and the HVO in Vares decided, at the beginning of September, that it had to find ways and means of bringing in humanitarian aid to the municipality of Vares and, at the same time, to see to the seriously ill, the elderly from Kakanj to be placed in areas which were more secure, which were safer. In that respect, a decision was taken to try to contact the Serbs who, in the municipality of Vares, held the municipality under control in part, and the Croats and the Bosniaks had not had any conflicts with them up until then. The negotiations lasted about a month, a month and a half, and the result of those negotiations was that an agreement had been reached to have a first convoy leave from Vares at the end of August and to bring humanitarian aid and three buses to take the people who were seriously ill and the infirm and elderly from the area of Herzegovina. This convoy was to pass through the Republika Srpska area, cross Zvornik towards Dervan and enter Livno, and this journey would last for about fifteen days, and the Serbs were paid for allowing this free passage, and it was paid a very high price, I might say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were supplies more readily available then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with that first convoy, a considerable number of refugees left, and the situation improved somewhat because the convoy included 64 trucks, and these trucks brought all the necessary food, and the situation improved. After this convoy, we had other convoys, so that the situation did improve. The shops began to function again. The Croatian Defence Council's doors opened, and the convoys brought in substantial quantities of commodity goods such as coffee, cigarettes, alcoholic beverage, et cetera. From that moment on, trade began with the Tuzla base in the Gradacac area, the Brcko area, the Tuzla area, and this was an area mostly populated by the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this trade evolve? We have the Croatian Defence Council with its own shop. Did private shopkeepers have shops, and what did the Bosniaks give in return?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the HVO with a chain of stores, private enterprises also had stores, and this trade was normal based on economic principles. Goods were paid for in cash, in coal in Banovica (phoen) and Tuzla, in salt, which was later transported to Herzegovina, and a portion was used for food for the winter, road service, for schools, hospitals, barracks, and so on because at that time everything suddenly began functioning normally. All the schools were open. All children went to school, both from the Bosniak villages and from the Croat villages. Transport was organised for the children and for anybody else, and everything functioned as it did in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council and its chain of stores and the shopkeepers and others, did they trade with the army of BH from Tuzla, and did they expect a certain amount of protection from that area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the representatives of the 2nd Corps of the army of BH and the Croatian Defence Council, the 115th Zvinski Division from Tuzla, because supplies were going via them, there was no line established towards the northern regions of Vares and the municipality of Olovo where the area of responsibility came under the 2nd Corps, and the situation there was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 17th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of October, 1993, a convoy arrived, and I think there were about 104 trucks and buses in that convoy, and they were to pull out the refugees, Croats, from Kakanj via the Serbian territory towards Herzegovina, to relocate them in safer areas because the people were in collective centres in Vares, and winter was coming on, and it was not possible to ensure the necessary supplies and care for those people. And so on the 17th of October, it was a Sunday, everybody boarded the convoy, and when the convoy was formed in the place called Ponikve above Vares where the staff of the HVO existed, and on the 17th of October, it reached Vares. And I think that Colonel -- he was Colonel at the time, Mr. Ivica Rajic arrived to take one of the able men in a battalion via Serbian territory to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next on that same night in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the problems that recruits had in passing across the territory of the Republika Srpska, the convoy, which was to take the recruits from Kakanj to Kiseljak, and the convoy for Herzegovina remained where it was, and on that night, at 6.30 p.m., the BH units attacked the lines of the Croatian Defence Council in the Lijesnica valley. Two members of the HVO were killed. One was arrested, that is to say, he disappeared. The lines were broken through, and that was, in fact, the beginning of the war in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That took place on the 17th of October, 1993, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of October, 1993, you leave for Herzegovina. Would you explain to the Trial Chamber where you went and why you went?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of October, once again in the morning, in the early morning, I came to the staff headquarters in Vares of the HVO to depart on that day, and the Muslim forces attacked the village of Kopjari and took control of it for a brief period of time. The situation was a chaotic one. Some people in the staff headquarters maintained that there were a lot of people, that the attack was launched by many men, and that we would not be able to defend ourselves. On that same day, between 2.00 p.m. and 3.00 p.m., Colonel Ivica Rajic left in the direction of Kiseljak and took with him Mr. Borivoje Malbasic, the former commander of the Vares brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you left for Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you return to Central Bosnia and where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, I left for Herzegovina on the 18th of October, 1992, on the evening, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you speak a little more slowly, please, and try to make pauses between your sentences?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I left in the evening with the task of taking the convoy of refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Interpreters say question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of October, 1992, I left for Herzegovina. My task was to escort the convoy carrying the refugees to Stolac and to bring a certain quantity of food necessary and other things necessary for the municipality of Vares. However, in Herzegovina and Siroki Brijeg I remained until the 26th of November, 1993, when I was to return to Kiseljak, because in the meantime Vares fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're in Herzegovina now, did you have any contact with the people in Vares? And if you did, how did you maintain those contacts? Would you explain this to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was in Siroki Brijeg, that was where the Vares HVO had its representative offices, and thanks to the fact that in the village of Dastansko in the Vares municipality, the locality was known as Jelina Kuce, we had a mobile phone which was functioning before the conflict, and it was Vares's only link with the world. And I was able to contact people every day using this mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that village, for the whole of the Vares municipality, the mobile phone was there. The transcript says you left Vares in 1992, whereas you meant, I think, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we'll correct that in the transcript, thank you. And what information did you get? You had daily contacts, several times a day, and what information from Vares did you receive when you were in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I had daily contact, I spoke several times a day with the people from the HVO, and most often with the security chief, Mr. Zvonko Duznovic. The information was that in Vares -- that is the first information I received was on the 18th of October, that a policeman at the HVO was killed. The next information we received was on the 21st of October, 1992 -- 1993, yes, I'm sorry, but not from Mr. Zvonko Duznovic, the information this time came from a young man working with the Mobitel in the Dastansko village. And he said that in Vares on the 21st of October, 1993 Colonel Ivica Rajic had arrived, and that in Vares the civilian HVO authorities were under arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who arrested these civilian authorities at the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Emil Harah, who at that time was the commander of the Bobovac Brigade. On the 21st of October, he called Ivica Rajic to assist him to stabilise the defence lines which were attacked by the BH army. That same day, when Mr. Rajic came to the HVO headquarters at Vares, he invited the representatives of the civilian authorities, the HVO of Vares and members of its presidency, to reach an agreement. And when they were discussing matters, the head of the police, Ivica Gavran, and the head of SIS, Zvonko Duznovic, were arrested and transferred by Serb territory to Kiseljak. And the other two presidents of Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Ante Pejcinovic, and the member of the presidency, Mr. Pavao Vidovic, were kept imprisoned at the headquarters in Ponikve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Rajic come alone or was he accompanied by Maturica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: He came to Vares accompanied by Maturicas units, with the objectives of stabilising the lines in Vares, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the commander of the brigade from Vares of the HVO, were there any changes there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, on the 21st these people were arrested, and on the 22nd a decision was reached to replace Emil Harah, the head of the Bobovac unit, and he appointed as head of the Bobovac brigade, Kresimir Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivica Rajic, as the Commander in Chief, the superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear later? What happened? Why did these replacements take place? Why did these arrests take place? Because this is not customary, not even in Bosnia, really.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of October, 1993, when I heard this piece of information, the brother of the president of Vares HVO, Ante Pejcinovic, or rather his brother, Bosko Pejcinovic, called me and he confirmed these people were arrested, and he asked me to intervene with the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, to see why they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear? What was this, politics, or what?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard later that the motive, when I came to Kiseljak and Herzegovina, and later as I was leaving, I heard that allegedly this was smuggling and trade with the Tuzla basin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to see Mate Boban, tell us about this event. What did you hear about over there and why did you go to see Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I went to see Mate Boban in Grude in order to see why they were arrested, and I took with me the deputy president of Vares, Mr. Zvonko Duznovic, who was with me down there, and the representative for the economy, Kruno Ridzic. But I asked them to come with me, but they didn't want to see Mr. Boban, because when they heard that these men were arrested, they were afraid for their own safety. And thanks to this, or rather, Mr. Vladislav Pogac was head of Mr. Boban's office, and he was from Vares, his father was from Vares, rather. I managed to see President Boban immediately, and talked to him. The first thing I told him was the following. I said, "Mr. President, in Vares the president of the HVO, Vares, Ante Pejcinovic, was arrested, and the members of the municipal HVO." And his reaction was the following. "No one is to arrest the president of the HVO unless I give such orders." I took the number of the mobile phone, and in front of me he phoned the village of Dastansko on the mobile phone. And when he asked whether Ante Pejcinovic, president of the HVO for Vares, was arrested, this man who was working on the mobile phone, his name is Ljudevit, he said, "Yes, it is true and he is locked up in the staff in Ponikve." After this conversation Mr. Boban told me that he would then call Mr. Petkovic in Kiseljak to see what was going on in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is General Petkovic, head of the main staff of the Croatian Defence Council; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boban talked to Mr. Petkovic, and as far as I could hear, the only question was, "Please tell me, check out what is going on in Vares and why was Ante Pejcinovic arrested." I did not hear what Mr. Petkovic answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it occur to you or president Boban to get in touch with Blaskic, who was the main commander over there in Central Bosnia? If it did not occur to you, why did it not occur to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Boban called Petkovic immediately, and he did not mention then Colonel Blaskic or anybody else from the Vitez area. He only called Petkovic, and he told him, he asked him to check what was going on in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this intervention of Boban vis-a-vis General Petkovic who was in Kiseljak, was it successful?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: It was only the next day that I found out that very same evening Ante Pejcinovic, the president of the HVO, was released, as well as Mr. Vidovic, who was a member of the HVO. And that very same evening through a local television the president of the HVO, Ante Pejcinovic, addressed the population, and he said that there should be no panic and that everything is under control and the situation was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of information was coming from the town of Vares, and what kind of information reached you? Practically, Rajic, with the assistance of Maturica, had made a coup d'etat, carried out a coup d'etat, figuratively speaking, and what was going on in the town of Vares itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In town the situation was rather tense. All the military conscripts, after Rajic came, were mobilised, those who were not mobilised, I mean. It is only natural the people were worried. And already on the 23rd, in the morning, when I called the mobile telephone company again, another person answered the phone, Mr. Zamko Barkic (phoen), who said that in Vares that morning an action was launched by Rajic, or rather Maturica, to arrest Muslims in Vares, and they were taken into school halls under the pretext that they had weapons. And allegedly these people had found their weapons and they took it to the barracks in Zabrezje. And at the same time, in Stupni Do, a cleansing activity had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were only weapons taken from Muslim apartments, or were these apartments perhaps looted, too? Was the Muslim population robbed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I found out in Kiseljak, from our people who were refugees, that during these arrests, the soldiers took away various equipment, jewelry, gold, took away their cars, and through Serbian territory they took it to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about Stupni Do? You were far away in Herzegovina, but through the mobile telephone company what kind of information did you receive?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The information I received then was simply that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please say question and answer. And I ask the witness to take it a bit more slowly. We're not so familiar with all this, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, we shall move on to a different area now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, please, let us try to take small breaks between our questions and answers, so that the interpreters can catch all of this properly. So, as I said, or rather, I will repeat the question that remained as my last question. What is the information that you received in Herzegovina through the mobile telephone company on the events in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I received information that fighting was taking place, and that this was the second day of fighting, and that Stupni Do could not be taken. After that, I received information that the action was completed, and it was a Sunday, by noon, I think, and this was the first information I received, and while I was in Herzegovina I did not receive any other information about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let us link this up to your return to Kiseljak. Did you get any supplementary information about Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from our people I received information that over there in Stupni Do civilians lost their lives, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after Stupni Do with the Maturica? Did they stay in the municipality of Vares or did they withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Although they came to reinforce the frontline, they withdrew that very same afternoon from the municipality of Vares, towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what happened on the 30th of October, 1993 in Vares, to the best of your information, that is the information that you were receiving in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of October an all out attack of the BH army started against the defence lines of the Bobovac Brigade in Vares from all directions, under pressure from Sarajevo. The forces of the 2nd Corps of the BH army from Tuzla joined in this attack, as well. On the 30th of October, the village of Dubastica was attacked and taken, intensive shelling took place of Gornji and Donja Borovica, and the civilian population from those areas fled to Vares. Also from the village of Ocevi and Supni Vijak (phoen), all of it came to the urban centre of the town of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court, how long did the fighting take place, and how long did the defence of Vares take place from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, until what date?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The defence of the municipality of Vares from the BH army took place until the 2nd of November, 1993, in the area of Perun, where the HVO forces were concentrated. The lines broke down, there was general chaos, and also in the village of Pogar. And between the 2nd and 3rd of November 1993, a decision was reached to evacuate the civilian population from the town of Vares itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, first, where were the civilians evacuated to? How many civilians, Croats, were escaping and how many were staying on in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the village of Dastansko and the village of Brgule, which is on the territory of the Serb republic and through the Serb entity towards Kiseljak and Kresevo. Part of them went in the direction of Sokolac too, in Republika Srpska. And they were set up in some kind of refugee camp there, but subsequently they were taken to Kiseljak. From Vares, during the night between the 2nd and 3rd of November, 1993, and on the 3rd of November, about seven and a half thousand Croats fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croats stayed in the municipality of Vares after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: 914 Croats remained in the municipality of Vares. And also in a part of the Vares municipality where they were holding the line, 1.600 HVO soldiers remained, because the Serbs, of course, would not let them pass through their territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in this short conflict with the Serbs, sorry, with the Muslims, for these past, for those few days, how many soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In the fighting with the BH army, 63 members of the Croatian Defence Council, the municipality of Vares were killed, and most of them were killed in the area of Perun, on the 2nd of November, 30 of them, and in the village of Pogar, 11 of them. And subsequently, after these killed soldiers were exchanged, it was established that many were taken prisoner first and then killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now chronologically we are going to stop for a while and then we are going to go back to this. But now, briefly, we go to a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps we could take a break now, since you're changing subjects. We're going to take a 20-minute break and we will start again at 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we said we would move to another area, commanders of the HVO brigade in Vares. Who was the first commander of the HVO brigade in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The first commander of the HVO Bobovac Vares Brigade was Mr. Borivoje Malbasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and who replaced him and why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, Mr. Malbasic, as the commander of the Bobovac Vares Brigade, sent a letter to the civilian HVO in Vares in which he expressed his dissatisfaction. He was asking to be paid for his work, a salary for his work, a large apartment for his family, and as the HVO of Vares was not able to comply with his request, and Mr. Borivoje Malbasic was given to alcohol intake, the civilian HVO of Vares decided that Mr. Malbasic should be replaced in his duty of commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who then became the commander after him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade, the Bobovac Vares Brigade, became Mr. Emil Harah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him, when, and why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: He was replaced on the 23rd -- on the 22nd, I'm sorry, of October, 1993 by Colonel Ivica Rajic, and he appointed as brigade commander Kresimir Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who appointed Kresimir Bozic and who then became commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Kresimir Bozic was appointed by Ivica Rajic, and he was the commander up until the time the Croats left Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of November, he left for Kiseljak, and he became the coordinator of the Bobovac Vares Brigade in Kiseljak, and Borivoje Malbasic was appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who appointed Borivoje Malbasic as commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed by Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us proceed with the chronology of the events. Your municipality of Vares and the inhabitants fled to Kiseljak. You returned from Herzegovina on the 26th of November, 1993 to Kiseljak, together with the convoy. Can you tell us whether, while Vares was still surrounded, that is, until the downfall of Vares, did you attempt to return to Vares with the convoy, and did anybody stop you in doing so? If so, why and who?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: We tried, on several occasions, while Vares was surrounded and while the fighting was still going on, to return to Vares. However, at first, we were not allowed -- we were not able to obtain the necessary quantities of fuel for the return journey. When we ensured the fuel necessary, we were not able to get permission by the Serbs for free passage across their territory, so that in actual fact, for 40 days, the drivers of the convoy spent 40 days out in the open at the broken down bridge in Capljina. I personally took them bread so that they should have something to eat from Medjagorja (phoen), from a humanitarian organisation there, and it is called "Bread for the Children," that particular humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how did you go back and how did you negotiate the terms for your return?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, I tried in Citluk with General Stanko Matic to negotiate the safe passage of the convoy, but we were not successful in this. And then by telephone I talked to Mr. Rajic, and after that, we were assured a safe passage, a safe passage for the convoy up to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from Herzegovina, did you use a normal telephone to talk to Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a normal, ordinary telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "normal," I'm not thinking of a mobile phone but the other type of telephone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I just discussed the passage of the convoy to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Kiseljak, what happened to you? What duties did you perform, and tell us of the situation you found when you returned to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Kiseljak, I met the coordinator of the Bobovac Vares Brigade, Mr. Kreso Bozic, who then took me to Colonel Ivica Rajic at the barracks in Kiseljak. And it was there that I was told to take over the command of the civilian HVO in Kiseljak, the HVO of Vares, with its headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties, in fact, in the situation there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: That I had to deal with the refugee Croats, their care and detention, that is to say, the Croats who were located in the collective centres in Kiseljak and Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Kiseljak related to the head of SIS, Duznovic, and his colleague Gavran?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the evening that I arrived in Kiseljak with the convoy, through a friend of mine, a lady friend, she worked at the radio station in Kiseljak, I learned that Mr. Duznovic and Mr. Gavran were in prison in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: They had been arrested, once again, by Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the charge against them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Allegedly, they had been taken to protect them from the HVO Vares soldiers who had run amuck, who were enraged, and who found themselves in a very difficult sandwich situation, positioned between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The head of SIS, Duznovic and Gavran, were later released. Duznovic was an ordinary private soldier. Can you tell us briefly what happened with the head of SIS from Vares? What did you hear about these events?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, when I returned to Kiseljak, in the meantime, the president of the HVO Vares up until that time, Ante Pejcinovic, had left Kiseljak by helicopter, had gone to Grude. And probably after his talk with Boban, Gavran and Duznovic were released from prison. Mr. Rajic deployed them as ordinary soldiers in the units that existed there. With his family, Mr. Duznovic was sent to a collective centre housed in the primary school in Lepenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next to Duznovic? What did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of February, 1994, he was taken away, and later on, I learned that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took him away?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: He was taken away by the HVO soldiers from Kiseljak, and his wife was told that he was being sought after by Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for his killing; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The real reason was probably the fact that Mr. Duznovic knew a great deal about the events that were going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the functioning of the overall power or authority in Kiseljak. At the time when you arrived, the government had been functioning for some time. Describe to us how it functioned in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: When I took over as commissioner of the HVO in Kiseljak, I was told that every evening at the barracks in Kiseljak meetings were being held of military commanders and civilian presidents of the HVO of Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, and that I was to join them from Vares. And from that time on, right up till the signing of the Washington Accords, every evening at 7.00 p.m., I was present at the meeting in the barracks at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conclude that the way in which the authorities functioned had been functioning for several months before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was told this by my colleagues, the presidents of the HVO. They said that this kind of power and authority had been established as soon as the conflict had broken out in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, how this unified military and civilian government functioned. Who presided? Who brought in the decisions? Describe the atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings were presided over by Colonel Ivica Rajic, and at these meetings, the members discussed all essential issues pertaining to the functioning of daily life in the area. This ranged from military actions to civilian needs and lodging for the refugees, the departure of the convoys, and so on and so forth. In a word, we could say that we were all there to execute the tasks assigned us by Mr. Rajic for individual segments and departments, and nothing could be done without him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say then that Ivica Rajic combined the civilian and military component of power and authority in his person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, where the refugees from Vares were housed, lodged. Were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The Vares refugees, in the beginning, were lodged in collective centres. In sports halls where there were over 500 people, they were on the floors and everywhere in the sports halls. As it was winter, the refugees were dissatisfied with the conditions, their housing conditions, and many said that there were empty flats that they could go to and empty houses belonging to Croats in Kiseljak and that the refugees were not allowed to take up residence in them, at least the families with small children and elderly family members. Then a decision was made by Mr. Rajic, and I was ordered to put it into effect, that is to say, that I should talk to our people and to put them up in the devastated Bosniak houses in Kiseljak, that is to say, in the surroundings of Kiseljak, and these houses were on the frontlines towards the BH army. People refused this and asked that they be taken from Kiseljak to safer areas. For this reason, we too had to come on several -- we were faced with a situation whereby we were not able to put these orders into effect, and our lives were jeopardised in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Interpreter, please say "question" and "answer."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present over a period of time and attended the regular daily meetings that were held at Mr. Rajic's when he issued orders to the military and civilians alike.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever hear of the fact that Rajic referred back to an order given by Colonel Blaskic? Did he mention any Blaskic orders at the meetings where all the important decisions were taken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As I say, I was present at all the meetings that took place, and when I was present, not a single order had come in from Colonel Blaskic. It was not read out at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Rajic ever mention Blaskic in any context during these official meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were friends with people who were Rajic's co-workers, assistants, either military or civilian. Could you explain to the Court what you heard about the relationship between Rajic and Blaskic, and what were they saying about Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was friends with friends and co-workers of Colonel Rajic's, and I got the impression during that period that Mr. Rajic, how should I put this, was holy to these people in Kiseljak. If it weren't for him, they couldn't have survived. That was the opinion of these people, that he was a true fighter. And when I talked to them, I found out that before him in Kiseljak, Colonel Blaskic was in command in Kiseljak. And then Bilalovac was taken by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the communication line between Kiseljak and Busovaca was thus cut off, and they were convinced that had Rajic been there this never would have happened. That is what I heard then. And also, when the situation was the most difficult in Vitez, before Christmas 1993, some commanders said that had Rajic been there, the situation would have been like in Kiseljak. Since I was not close to Colonel Blaskic and I did not know him as a military man, I must admit that I also got the impression, then, according to the stories that they told, that this was a soldier who was not capable of commanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that Rajic, for the army and the people of Kiseljak, that he was absolutely holy to them, what are you trying to say? That he was an absolute leader? Explain to the Court what did you mean by saying "holy"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I already said nothing could have been done without him. When a convoy was formed, in order to evacuate the old and the ill from Kiseljak, we were given an assignment. I was told that there would be 12 buses of refugees from Vares. I was told to make lists and to bring them to him, and that only after Mr. Rajic saw these lists people got the green light, so to speak. He was the one who left some people on the lists, and those whose names were crossed out by him, they could not leave. If any kind of incident occurred on the part of irresponsible individuals, I'm referring to soldiers, the only person who could calm down these individuals and the only person who could actually have them locked up, if necessary, was Colonel Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we shall move into a different area which we have not touched until now, intentionally so, and that is the following. What about the villages of the municipality of Vares that the Croats had abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move on to that, I would like to have a document distributed, and could you please give me the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D440, D440A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So could you tell us who wrote this document, in what capacity, and who was it sent to, and at whose request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I wrote this document as president of the municipal council of Vares. It is addressed to Mr. Nobilo and it contains a chronology of the suffering of the Croatian people in the municipality of Vares in the period from the 3rd of November, 1993. The document was made on the basis of information gathered from the officials of the Vares municipality, or rather, the members of the war crimes commission of Herceg-Bosna, and also the Vares Dastansko police force, also from the Vares Vijak Borovica priest, and also on the basis of eyewitness statements. It contains this entire subject matter: The killing and suffering of civilians, the destruction of cemeteries and churches, and the destruction of family homes and entire villages that were rased to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that on the basis of the methodology you applied in the municipality of Vares all this information is reliable and true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: One can say they are one hundred per cent correct and true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go through this document a bit, although it speaks for itself. We are going to skip the civilian casualties. On page 7 there is a title "Churches, chapels and cemeteries," so could you please tell the Court about some of the greater devastations of Catholic cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the devastation of Catholic churches, chapels, cemeteries, the most difficult situation was in the parish of Borovica. The local church in the village of Gornja Borovica, together with the priest's home, was torched, looted, and now it is in ruins, the church is in ruins, and also it looks like a dump. The big cross from the church tower was thrown in front of the door to the church. I first saw this myself on the 6th of August, 1994, and the only thing one could see in the church were burned pews, a broken altar and remains of the aluminium roof that had burned down. Also, in the village of Gornja and Donja Borovica, the chapels were looted, and also the crosses were broken on all these chapels. In Borovicke Njive, a small hamlet belonging to the parish of Borovica, the chapel at the local cemetery was also demolished, and a few tombstones as well. In the neighbouring village of Kopljari, which was the first to be destroyed, the Catholic cemetery was desecrated and firearms were used to shoot at the tombstones. All the iron crosses were broken, and some were even throw out of the cemetery. Three monuments were completely destroyed. The chapel was demolished and damaged, and it was damaged in the following way: A tree fell, a tree that was right next to it fell, and that is how it demolished it. In another Catholic village, Dubastica, as the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina entered the village, the chapel was forcefully opened and all the items belonging to the church were scattered all about. In the village of Mir, which is in the immediate vicinity of Stupni Do, on two occasions Muslim soldiers desecrated the cemetery, and the last desecration of the cemetery occurred afterwards, in peacetime, in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of November, 1996, when the chapel and 60 tombstones were completely demolished, all the wooden and iron crosses were broken, as well as the tombstones themselves. During this same night, between the 2nd and 3rd of November, in the neighbouring village of Bijelo Borje, the chapel was desecrated, too. It was damaged, the church items were scattered all about, and 14 tombstones were broken. All the crosses, wooden and metal, were broken and scattered all about. I saw this myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we don't have to go into all these details, because we have this document.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give us the locations where similar things happened, in terms of Catholic churches and Catholic cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Also in the parish of Vijak, the parish church was forcefully opened, the church items were scattered all about, the priest's home was looted, and the members of the BH army closed the cattle in it as they were looting these villages. Also in the village of Krcevine, on the bell tower there are marks, obviously the bell was shot at. And also the cross that is in the centre of the village was broken. The same fate was suffered by the chapel in the village of Ocevi where the cross was carried away and it was turned into a dump. And then in the village of Pogar, where two grenades were fired at the church. And also in Vares Majdan, the Catholic church of Saint Barbara was forcefully opened, and relics were thrown all around the floor. Nothing was taken away, but the place was in shambles. The church of the parish of Vares was, suffered the most destruction, that was in the village of Brezik. The members of the BH army used it as a position against the HVO, so they fired from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have all the other details and all the other locations in the document. Now, we shall move on to Croatian villages. Let us see what the situation was like there. But before that we would like to distribute, a map of the JNA of Vares for one to 50.000. And as this map is being distributed, could you please tell us who made these marks on the map? And what do they actually represent?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I did this. I made these marks on the map, and these are Croatian villages in the municipality of Vares that were harmed in various ways as the BH army came into Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have a different kind of map, on this map of Vares 4, not all of it is depicted, so that is why we added this other copy, and this is in addition to the big map. So we have a big map and a small map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D441.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is a big map and small map that go together.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I understand this correctly, we're receiving two large maps, and they are different in respect of the notes on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The original is two large maps, the copies of each set consist of one large map and then only a portion of the second large map, because only a small part of it is marked. They will fit together for reference purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want the same number to be on the small and the large one? That's what you mean, isn't it, Mr. Hayman? In other words, the D442 will be the large map, to which the small one is added; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe they will be D441 and D441A for the small map, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right, but the other maps are not annotated in that same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, Mr. Dubuisson? The map that you're giving to the OTP, that's 441; isn't it? This one, is that right? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's different. Mr. President, there are two maps in the original that we give to the registrar, and they should be included in the files. Together they comprise the municipality of Vares. However, the copies are one entire big map and a small photocopy of another map. With your permission, I would like to show this. This is the first map and this is a photocopy of the other map, but together we tender this as a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, it should be numbered with the same number; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we are not giving the registrar the photocopy, we are giving him the original of the big map, and everybody else is being given a small map and a big map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we do it that way, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, no problem, says the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please put one map on the ELMO? Yes, one map, it's better another map. And then we can move it. Put the monitor on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, is everything in order now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, we are trying to sort this out. Please, could you enlarge it? Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pejcinovic, your document, page 10, let us use that, and use the pointer and show on the ELMO this village. And could you explain what happened in each and every one of these villages?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Gornja Borovica, then Donja Borovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please keep your pointer there, and as you hold the pointer there, tell us what happened in that village.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Donja Borovica, the following thing happened. After the withdrawal of the army and civilians, a number of civilians remained, nevertheless, there, and they were victims. And as far as buildings are concerned, in the village of Borovica, or in the parish of Borovica, which consists of Donja Borovica and Gornja Borovica, these are two villages, and you can see them on the small map, before the war there were 262 households, Croat households. Three hundred forty family homes were torched and 750 other buildings, such as sheds, stables, barns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let us move on to the village of Kopljari. It's on the other map. Could we change the map, please? Yes, that's the map. So on the other map is the village of Kopljari. So please let us show this on the ELMO. Please put your pointer there. All right. And what happened in the village of Kopljari?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Kopljari was taken by the BH army on the 21st of October, 1993. Before the war it had a population of 150 persons, all of them Croats. During the first assault -- actually I have to say that the village was taken twice, the first time on the 18th of October, when only two houses were torched, and the second time on the 21st of October when the entire village was rased to the ground. And later on, a survey was made in order to reconstruct the municipality of Vares, and we realised that 60 family houses were burned down, and all the other buildings, all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you show Borovicke Njive with your pointer, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
