utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would be unaware of helicopter landing sites in Busovaca or Vitez, yourself, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No? Does that mean you're not aware of helicopter landing sites in Busovaca or Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of helicopter landing sites in Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that after the 26th of October, 1993, you were involved in regular meetings in Kiseljak with Ivica Rajic and other officials in the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: From the 27th of November, I mean, on the 26th, I arrived in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those regular meetings ceased at the Washington Agreement, at the time of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in those meetings, was the military situation in Kiseljak and Central Bosnia regularly discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: At meetings all problems were discussed that were related to the Kiseljak Kresevo enclave. The other areas in Central Bosnia were not referred to very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, was the military situation in Kiseljak discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but not in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the frontlines of the confrontation between the HVO and the ABiH discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Since I had come to Kiseljak I was not very familiar with these frontlines, so I wasn't really very interested in this. So all of that was foreign to me, when this was discussed, I mean the frontlines and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that Muslim prisoners of war and civilians were used to dig HVO trenches on those frontlines?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a Defence witness who testified two weeks ago, a Catholic priest, Father Pervan; do you know Ivan Pervan?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he infrequently attended the meetings which you are speaking of with Mr. Rajic, and he stated that trench digging was a matter that was regularly discussed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence witness is being misinterpreted. He said he would come to see Ivica Rajic in the afternoon for coffee, and he did not say that he would attend these evening meetings at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, was it a meeting where they were just drinking coffee, or was it a strategic meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether the witness discussed hot beverages at the meeting, to be honest, Mr. President. I do recall that he certainly stated that he attended a number of these meetings and he raised the matter of trench digging with both General Petkovic and Colonel Rajic. That is my recollection of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My recollection, for what it's worth, Mr. President, is he met with Rajic, sometimes at his house, sometimes at the barracks, but they were personal meetings, they were not meetings of a larger military or civil group of authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will ask the witness. Thank you, Mr. Hayman, we will ask the witness. What kind of meeting was it? Did you meet regularly to drink coffee, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would meet every evening at 7.00 p.m. for work meetings. At these meetings we did not drink coffee, but Father Ivan Pervan never attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, I think it's clear now. Thank you. Mr. Cayley, would you modify your question, please, accordingly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, at these meetings in Kiseljak, was the matter of the use of Muslim prisoners of war and civilians for forced trench digging discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times during this time period did you visit the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Every evening meeting were held at 7.00 p.m. at the barracks in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware during that time period as to whether or not Muslim prisoners of war were being kept in the barracks at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: When I would come to these meetings I would report to the guard at the entrance and then I was escorted by him to the command of the barracks in Kiseljak, and that is exactly the way I would go back. I did not walk around the barracks otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there had been Muslim prisoners of war in other buildings apart from the headquarters building, you would not have been aware of their presence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them, so that is why I cannot say that they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to go to other buildings within the Kiseljak barracks apart from the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No, because there was no need for me to go around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your examination-in-chief that a number of people in Kiseljak said that had Colonel Rajic been in command in January of 1993, Bilalovac would not have fallen; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command in Kiseljak in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what they said, when Bilalovac fell the commander was Mr. Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic, and who was that in January, 1993, that I could not say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Bilalovac fall?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I know that when the conflict broke out in Central Bosnia, this was sometime in mid-April, so it might have been in May. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware that Bilalovac fell to the Bosnian army in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that a number of people stated to you that Blaskic was not capable as a commander; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was subsequently promoted to the command of the HVO, in fact, as we have previously discussed in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that the authorities in Mostar had a different view of Blaskic's military ability than those individuals in Kiseljak that were speaking to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the view of the authorities in Mostar was, but I spoke about the informal conversations I had in the "couloirs" among Rajic's closest associates and the commanders of his units. And the only true fighter for them was Ivica Rajic. They did not even recognise Milvoj Petkovic or Tihomir Blaskic as a true fighter, not anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the chitchat that was taking place between friends and colleagues in Kiseljak, this was the discussion on Colonel Blaskic's military capability?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: These were conversations with the closest associates of Ivica Rajic that were in charge of various areas, and this was before the formal meetings. Before the meeting we would talk, and then they would say that the only true commander of the Croatian Defence Council for the Croatian people, the only one who knows how to defend them, and this is quite obvious in Kiseljak, is Mr. Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name those people with whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: There were many names, but these were the closest associates of his. I could not recall all their names, and there were at least 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name the closest associates of whom you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew some of them by their names, and others I only knew their nicknames. I was never really interested in what was their first name or their last name, because they didn't ask me about my first name or last name, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, you met with these people every night; are you telling the Judges you didn't know what they were called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that I didn't know what they were called. I said that I knew many of them by their nicknames, and only some of them by their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Name them. Name the people that you spoke with.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that, but I don't know what it will mean to you if I say Dzuna, Kopa, so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Name some of these people with whom you spoke.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know their real names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony to the Judges is that the persons with whom you spoke about General Blaskic's military ability, you didn't know what their real names were and that you met these people every night?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The answer was "yes," Mr. President. The witness said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course he said "yes," but before that, he told you the names of those individuals. Everybody knows who Cona is, and you should too, and Dzuna, everybody over there knows who Dzuna is, and they all know them by those nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know when Ivica Rajic was appointed to the command in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me refresh your memory. If the witness could be shown Exhibit 456, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/62. Have you had the opportunity to read it, Mr. Pejcinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that on the 4th of July, 1992, Colonel Blaskic appointed Ivica Rajic as his representative in Operative Zone number 3; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Operative Zone covered the municipalities of Busovaca, Fojnica, Kiseljak, Kresevo, Kakanj, and Vares; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your examination-in-chief that in November of 1993, Ivica Rajic was in command of the municipalities of Fojnica, Kiseljak, and Kresevo, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Kresevo -- Fojnica, Kiseljak, Kresevo, and Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in November of 1993, Vares had fallen to the Bosnian army, had it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, three villages were still under the control of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that time period, in November of 1993, Mr. Rajic was in command in Fojnica, Kiseljak, Kresevo, and in three villages in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Kiseljak, Kresevo, part of the Fojnica municipality under HVO control, and part of the Vares municipality under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Kakanj had come under Bosnian control, hadn't it, by November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Busovaca, although you won't know this, was moved to another Operative Zone; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a soldier, and so I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of who was in overall command of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone from September of 1992 to January of 1994, which included the areas that we've just discussed and a number of others which are listed in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Colonel Blaskic was the superior for these areas, but as far as the regions I mentioned, I maintain that this was only on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Pejcinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We mentioned language, although that is not the most important thing in the world for this particular case, but let's clarify the question of languages, Bosnian and Croatian. Before the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke out, that is to say, before 1992, what was the language called that you were taught at school in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The language was called Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, you are an educated man, in the 50 years of the existence of Yugoslavia, did the Bosnian language ever exist?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No, the Bosnian language never existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you throw out the word "Serbian" from the Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Serbs had carried out an aggression on the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, whatever has changed, did the teachers in the school teach the children the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Vares, the headmaster in Vares during the HVO and today is Mrs. Senija Karamehic, and she is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the teachers replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The only replacement were teachers of the Serb ethnic group that went to Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of the educational department, the number one man for education in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The number one man for education was Mrs. Mufida Dzindo, and she was a member of the Bozniak people. And Mrs. Mufida was appointed by decision of Mate Boban, president of the Croatian community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Suad Imamagic, Rusmir Berberovic, what ethnic group do they belong to and what were they members of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: They are Bosniak. One was in charge, Mr. Rusmir Berberovic was in charge of civil defence, and Mr. Suad Imamagic was in charge of the PTT communications and links, but later on he left that post, and he was appointed -- as I said, Dr. Edim Ascerija was the president for health matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, we're not going to introduce all these documents, how did you lose your job in the Vares mine?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I was sacked by decision of the commissioner of the Vares mines. And in this order, it states that I was no longer to perform my job as of the 2nd of November, 1993, and the explanation given was that I placed myself on the side of those hostile to the BH side as a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we then conclude that you lost your job for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I lost my job for political reasons and so did all the Croats, military-able men. They all received orders of this kind dismissing them, and the women and men who were not of military age and worked and went to Kiseljak and Kresevo, they were told that they would no longer be employed because they had not reported for duty for three weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor, you mentioned a letter of the commander of a Nordic battalion. Would you read out the relevant portions of that letter, very briefly? Give us the date. When did you receive the letter? Who sent the letter? Just the relevant portions of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. Mr. President, if the witness is going to read from a letter, we would like a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the Prosecution counsel should have the letter. That seems more proper to me. Perhaps the Judges should have it as well. At least the Prosecution counsel should. It has to do with character references; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, no. I don't have the letter. I have never seen the letter. It is the document belonging to the witness, and if he can read out a part of the letter, well and good. If not, we can skip over it and move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We should have sight of the letter, Mr. President, if the witness is reading from documents; just as when we ask questions of the witnesses, the documents are provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, we won't read the letter. We don't want to take up the Trial Chamber's valuable time. We desist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But will you tell us what is stated in the letter? What did the commander of the Nordic battalion tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: When I intervened --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness can say something that concerns him personally and that he not read the letter. What did you want to say? We're losing our patience here. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of December, 1993, I sent a letter via UNPROFOR to Kiseljak, to the commander of the Nordic Brigade of the United Nations which was stationed in Vares, and I received a reply on the 15th of December, 1993. In my letter, I mentioned several important facts which took place in the Vares municipality and the suffering and what the villages of Borovica Gornja and Dornja had suffered. Mr. Hakam Birger, the commander of the Nordic Battalion of the United Nations said as follows: "As far as the events in Borovica are concerned, one day after the fact that strong forces of the BH army took control of Borovica, I sent a patrol to that village. Several houses were burning in the village. The interior of the Catholic church had been devastated. We found one dead HVO soldier in the village. Seven days after that event, I sent a second patrol to the village of Borovica, and that patrol observed that the whole village, including the Catholic church, had been burnt to the ground. One day later," says Major Birger, "I personally visited Borovica and was touched and moved by what had happened there. On that occasion, my patrol found two dead soldiers, civilians, and took them to the U.N. hospital in Visoko." And finally, in a final paragraph, it says, "As far as the events in Borovica are concerned, I'm very sorry that the destruction of Borovica was not -- that as much attention was not paid to Borovica as it was to Stupni Do." And at the end of this letter, he goes on to state, "I have gained information that Vares for centuries was populated by the Bosnian Croats."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pejcinovic, please tell the Court, judging by what you know, until the present day, have you ever, ever heard of anyone being held accountable for burning some 20 villages and hundreds of Croatian houses and the looting of hundreds of Croatian family homes in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: For these murders, lootings and the killing of 14 civilians in the most abhorrent manner, nobody was ever held responsible, as if nothing had ever happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let us be quite clear on this, do you think that the fact that the unit came from Kiseljak that perpetrated the atrocity at Stupni Do and then withdrew from the municipality of Vares, and then withdrew from there; was that a provocation towards the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a provocation, but it was not the main reason why the BH army attacked Vares, because in their report they say the preparations for the attack on Vares started on the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There has been by a mistake in the interpretation, or maybe I have misspoke. This was a provocation, in my original question this was a provocation towards the Bosnians not the Croats, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pejcinovic. Perhaps I can have the benefit of your great knowledge of the situation to clarify a few points. You mentioned that Ivica Rajic was considered by the people you knew, and I quote the word you said in English, that he was considered as being holy. Holy, that reminds me of a saint or something. Now, would that exclude General Blaskic from the picture? Would that mean that Blaskic's authority was questioned, was disputed, and that his orders would not be obeyed and that he was not in control of the situation? Does the General need to be holy, too, or can he survive beside a holy person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as regards that, that everybody swore by Mr. Rajic in Kiseljak, that is true. He was considered to be an idol in terms of the Croatian defence in that enclave. And when somebody is fully surrounded, then it is quite logical that they accept that kind of a fact. And I said in my statement, on the basis of all these stories I came to the conclusion that General Blaskic, or rather Colonel Blaskic, was a very poor soldier. Because it is not that there was such an opinion of General Blaskic only, but all other officers of the Croatian Defence Council, up to the top officers the commanders in the main staff; because they thought that only Mr. Rajic was the person who could defend the Croatian people that were fully surrounded there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that prevent Colonel Blaskic at the time, prevent him from giving orders when necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, on the basis of everything that happened there, it would not have prevented him from doing it, but I don't think that those orders would have been followed, because I said what kind of an opinion existed concerning Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, perhaps your knowledge can extend. Tell me if some serious orders of Colonel Blaskic were, in fact, not followed because of his unpopularity, or anything of that, or his weakness, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: During the time I was in Kiseljak, at those meetings I never saw or heard a single order issued by Colonel Blaskic. I did not see any of his orders in writing. It is one simple fact, and that is that all orders were issued by Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are speaking only of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Of Kiseljak, Kresevo, part of the municipality of Fojnica, and part of the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You never saw an order by him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think, yourself, that the events in Stupni Do were horrific, and you confirmed what the Prosecutor said about burning 60 houses, or something like that, or you said it yourself, that 60 houses were burned. That was by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, granting, as you said, that you're not aware that orders had been given by Rajic to commit these atrocities, the fact that the soldiers were left to commit them, would that mean that they were under no serious control, or there was no serious attempt to prevent them from doing such things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: These were special purpose units, and they were under the command of Mr. Rajic, and I cannot claim that somebody had issued orders to someone to commit a crime, and I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, my question is: You don't know that somebody issued orders, but were the soldiers of the HVO at liberty to commit atrocities with impunity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as regards these units, the ones I mentioned, I can say quite freely that they were at liberty to act that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said they were under the jurisdiction of Rajic, or was it the jurisdiction of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Under the jurisdiction of Colonel Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Rajic was on equal footing with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I only know, I'm not very knowledgeable in these matters, but I know that the units were under the command of Mr. Rajic, because he was in Vares at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but in the chain of command, was Colonel Blaskic his superior at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know what these Operative Zones were like exactly, I'm not very knowledgeable in these matters, but I know that Colonel Blaskic was in command of the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in one of the documents which we had, I think it's D456, or something, the passage has been referred to by the Defence counsel, I don't find it in English, I have it in French, so, it says: "There is no Bosniak language, and this is an insult to the Croats to try to transform the Croatian language into any type of Bosnian language." Now, would that indicate that those who wrote this, I think it was the Croatian Defence Council, is denying the cultural identity of the Bosniaks? Language is a cultural identity; was that an expression of rejection of this cultural identity in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when that document was written, then indeed there was no Bosnian language, because there was not a single textbook in the Bosnian language from which one could teach. There were only textbooks in the Serbo-Croat or Croato-Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in a way there was no change in the school, in the school curriculum at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. By the way, are you related to Mr. Ante Pejcinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: We are not next of kin, we are distantly related. Half of Vares are Pejcinovics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, dreadful things happened in Vares. Before those things happened, would I be right in thinking that the position was this: That the two communities lived in harmony with each other, gradually, however, those harmonious relations soured and deteriorated; would that be a correct picture of the general situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I want you to think back to the period when relations between the two communities were harmonious. At that time what was the body in which authority resided?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, sometime until April, 1992, there was an assembly of the municipality of Vares, or assemblymen in the assembly of Vares were the legislative branch of government, and there was also an executive branch, that is to say, a municipal government that consisted of representatives of all three national groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And then you said in July, 1992 the HVO took authority in Vares. Do I recall your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Not in all of Vares, not in all of the municipality of Vares, but only in part of the Vares municipality which is populated by the majority Croat population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So the old arrangements went out and new arrangements came in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because the assembly no longer met. The representatives of the least numerous people in the municipality of Vares, those were the Serbs, they left all bodies of government in Vares, the legislative and executive, and also part of the villages of the municipality of Vares that were populated by Serbs seceded from Vares and joined Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Under the previous arrangements, did the Party of Democratic Action have a part?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the old system. In the new system, when the HVO took over, the Party of Democratic Action did not take part in government, but other representatives of the Bosniak people did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Why did the Party of Democratic Action not take part under the new dispensation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Because they thought that since the president of the municipal assembly, Dario Andric, had resigned, a Bosniak should come in his place, a Bosniak lady, to be precise, Mervana Hadjimurtezic, and that she should head the body which should be called the Presidency of the Municipality of Vares and which would replace the assembly in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I want you to think of the two communities on the ground, the Croats and the Muslims; were the Croats satisfied with the new arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were the Muslims satisfied with the new arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the majority, rather, 99 per cent of the Bosniak population that lived in the town of Vares, in the urban part of the town of Vares, stayed on. They remained in their homes, they continued going to school, to work, and also most of the pupils from Bosniak villages continued to go to school, and the teaching process evolved in 1992. And during this part of 1993, until the refugees from Kakanj came, the Croat refugees from Kakanj, it was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcinovic, I have listened to you, but I have to tell you that my impression is that that was not an answer to my question. People may stay on. My question is whether the Muslims were satisfied with the new arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot know, Your Honour, whether all of them were satisfied, but the ones I talked to were satisfied. And it is certain that there were some who were not satisfied, because had all of them been satisfied, a parallel government would not have been established of the Bosniak people in the village of Debro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you have discussed with us the language change. I ask you this question: How did the Muslim community at large interpret the language change? Did they see the change as intended to replace a language they had been accustomed to by another type of language, however related the two might be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the HVO was in power, there weren't any possibilities for carrying out a fundamental change of the existing language. This was a language with a few attempts made to introduce some Croat language, but the old textbooks were still there from the socialist system, and the teachers also from the old system, quite a few of them were Serbs who stayed on in Vares. It was impossible during one period of time, during a one-year period, to make such a drastic change. And it was only at the end of '93 and the beginning of '94 that textbooks first appeared in the Bosnian and Croatian languages. And finally in the Washington Constitution, that is to say, in the Constitution of the Federation, we had two equal languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, my impression from what you have been saying is that there was no real difference between the two languages; is that impression correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Linguistic experts say that it is a very slight difference, but it does exist, if we look at it carefully, but it's a very slight difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, if the difference was slight, only slight, why was the change made, and why was there insistence on making the change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, because the language that was spoken in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the war was called Serbo-Croat, but basically it had been the Serb language. And after the Serb aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, both the Croats and the Bosniaks could not accept a language which was an aggressor's language to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to the Lasva Valley. Rather, let us turn to an entity called Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Are you familiar with that term?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that the area which the term comprehended was a fairly large geographical area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But would you say that from the point of view of the HVO, it constituted a single military constituency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The area of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, Your Honour, could not, or rather could be a single military entity from a military point of view, but from the point of view of the territorial principle, this was impossible. The command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia included several enclaves where the Croats lived as the majority population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me, would military developments in one part of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia be capable of having an effect on the military situation in another part of the zone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, this was during 1993, but during 1992, at the beginning of 1993, the HVO was under a single command, but one could notice that the organisation of the defence was carried out exclusively according to the territorial principle in very small enclaves. There was not a single system of defence, and this was probably due to impediments in communication between the different enclaves and various problems. People within these enclaves probably organised themselves on their own and prepared themselves for fighting, for defence, and the result of this is that these Croatian enclaves fell one after the other into the enemy's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: Was the Kiseljak area, for example, one part only of the zone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was an Operative Group which was within the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, having a regard to the problems you have mentioned, was it necessary to have someone in authority who could coordinate actions in the various enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Theoretically viewed, Your Honour, there was a need for this, but it was very difficult to execute this in practical terms. If you have no physical contacts with your commanders, then it is difficult to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see the distinction you're making, but I understand you to say that precisely because of those local difficulties, it was, if only theoretically, necessary to have a central coordinator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was necessary to have that, and it was like that under normal conditions. But under conditions of a conflict when the territory of Central Bosnia was divided up into a series of small enclaves, it was practically impossible to organise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, who was that central coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the military part, Your Honour, then it should have been the command of this collective area. But because of the divided enclaves, Operative Groups were appointed, and individual commanders of those Operative Groups were the coordinators with the brigades, if that was at all possible as well, because it was impossible by telephone and by any other communication link to command from Kiseljak a brigade in Vares, which is at a distance of some 50 kilometres as the crow flies, let alone by road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, whatever the difficulties were, was there a central military coordinator in the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: On paper, yes, but I don't know how it functioned in practice. I was not a military man myself, and so I did not have direct contacts, Your Honour, with the coordinators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On paper, if only on paper, who was that central commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the collective zone, that is to say, of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Who was that commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, one last point: I gathered from what you said that there were refugees. The HVO took in the Croat refugees but arranged for the Muslim refugees to pass on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the area which I was linked to, the Vares municipality, in 1992, both the Croat and the Bosniak refugees were taken in, both Bosniaks from Sokolac, Han-Pijesak, part of the Olovo municipality, and some Croats from the Ilijas municipality. However, in 1993 when the refugees from Kakanj arrived, nobody was able to be put up in Vares anymore, whether they were Croats or Bosniaks. And in 1992, as the result of the Serbian aggression, the municipality of Vares took in, while it had the capacity to do so, both the Bosniak and the Croat refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was a stage reached when the HVO sent off the Muslim refugees but accommodated the Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality in which I lived, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have only one question to ask you. In your opinion, did General Blaskic have civilian powers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is my opinion that General Blaskic did not have civilian powers, that he was only a military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For example, he couldn't give any orders to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I think never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We spoke a great deal about his authority which apparently was not recognised, among others, by Ivica Rajic. From your point of view as an official in political matters for the HVO, did you recognise that he had any type of competence or authority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not understand who you were referring to, whether to Colonel Blaskic or Colonel Rajic. Who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps I didn't ask the question clearly. Let me ask it again. I thought that in that zone of command, Rajic was considered as the chief, even as more competent, more authoritative than the accused, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to ask you, you as an important political official, did you recognise that the accused had certain authority and jurisdiction or competence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: For Colonel Blaskic at that time, the time that I spoke about, I did not feel that he had any authority over those areas that we discussed here because, as I said, Your Honour, everything that took place in the enclave, all the decisions made, both civilian and military, the boss was Colonel Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were you surprised when that kind of responsibility was given to him, that is, to the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia? I suppose you must have been surprised.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were. Perhaps you can't answer this, but what factors do you think would have allowed the accused to have such confidence from the political authorities, because basically many people in high ranking positions were not competent, perhaps even in the military sphere. To what do you attribute that career at the time of so many complicated and difficult situations? What would have propelled him to such a high level of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it was the result of the fact that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have any educated officers, and so it was better to have any kind of educated officer than an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So he was named because, theoretically, he had been trained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that's it, yes. Because after all the stories and after all this talking, I'm talking about a part of Central Bosnia and the mood there, and I personally said during the examination-in-chief that I too doubted the competence of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, my last question: If everybody had doubts as to the military practical abilities of the accused for such a high command, would you be in agreement with me when I say that perhaps people trusted him because he thought the same way as the political project which was being developed by the Croatian leadership? Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your question but I don't know whether everybody believed, Your Honour, whether they all believed Colonel Blaskic. But I'm saying this and I'm speaking for the part where I was personally present, that in talking to people in my region, they did not have confidence in him. I don't know what it was like in the other enclaves because I never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you haven't completely answered my question. What I was trying to ask, asking you, you who were an official, a local, important official, I was wondering why, in such a difficult situation, in a war situation, the highest levels of the political authorities and command trusted such a high position to Colonel Blaskic? You're telling me that he was not recognised as being competent on the ground, and you're telling me that it's because he was theoretically competent. Well, I can understand that. He had gone to the military academy, and perhaps that's a bit skimpy when you're in a war situation. My question was to know whether you felt that he could have been appointed to that position because politically he may have agreed with all of the assertions that appear in the famous report which is covered by 456 and 475. If you can't answer, then don't. I'm not trying to force you to answer something.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PEJCINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot say because my competences are not as broad for me to be able to know why Mr. Colonel Blaskic was appointed to that post, to that position. I can only say, as a man, that it is different when somebody is appointed when you don't have a lot of problems in the region, and then the problems turn up, and then you see the positive and the negative aspects of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's where we will stop. The Tribunal would like to thank you for your contribution, which was a bit long and tiring, but all the more reason for me and my colleagues to wish you a good trip back home. We will suspend until 2.00 on Monday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's now 5.30. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
